[h3]Summary[/h3] The game is really good quality-wise, but I'm no longer the target demographic thus I can't recommend it. [h3]The good[/h3] The game has some really fun gameplay, fantastic scenary (it really feel like a theme-park ride) and breathe high quality in atmosphere, graphics, sound (cars, music and commentator) and it simply feels great to drive. [h3]The Bad[/h3] Starting the game you have to log into your MS-account, connect your accounts and connect to it whenever you start the game (I couldn't find a way to start the game without it). No big deal, but it was 5 minutes of direct annoyance and if my internet goes I can't boot the game. Playing for around 2 hours I got hit by 3 fullscreen splash screens that locked my game until I removed it, straight after a race, in-game, that tried to sell me the new game FH6, missing DLC etc. The in-game store is very noticable with "new notifications"-marks and it's part of the main menu. It felt like a mobile game in that regard. [h3]The Demographic[/h3] The game start with blasting off straight away, you get thrown into epic race scenes for about 5-10 minutes, which feel great, then you hit the character creation screen. It's a loud white and pink colored UI (which is the UI for the rest of the game). The first tab is to choose between very ethnically varied characters, next is genders including they/them... an two large tabs for choosing prosthetics and hearing aids... It's not a bad thing per se, but resources were spent on quite a lot of options that, to me, has no place in a racing game and is clearly catering to a certain crowd. After playing for 2 hours, I realized this was a theme. This game is very much trying to vibe with the "modern audiances" with bright colors and a chirpy attitude. I am not a fan of that. I wanted a simcade with muscle/super cars, high octane racing and a badass feel in a sleek upgraded package. I've realized I'm not the target demographic anymore, which is my issue and not the game being bad. However, it really pulls me out of the immersion. The Steam store pictures and trailers show none of this and all the focus is on cool cars going fast (in hindsight, the opening of the second trailer really hints at it). Thank god for Steam's refund policy.

Elden Ring to jedna z tych gier, które jeszcze przed premierą zostały wyniesione na piedestał. Produkcja studia FromSoftware, twórców serii Dark Souls, była zapowiadana jako rozwinięcie znanej formuły w otwartym świecie. Efekt końcowy jest jednak bardziej złożony. To gra z wieloma świetnymi pomysłami, ale jednocześnie z wyraźnymi problemami projektowymi, które często wpływają na komfort rozgrywki. System rozwoju postaci Jednym z największych atutów gry jest ogromna różnorodność buildów. Gracz może rozwijać postać na wiele sposobów, od klasycznego wojownika z ciężką bronią, przez szybkie buildy zręcznościowe, aż po potężne postacie oparte na magii. System rozwoju daje dużą swobodę i zachęca do eksperymentowania. Problem pojawia się jednak w trakcie rozgrywki. Dość często okazuje się, że build, który wcześniej działał bardzo dobrze, nagle przestaje być skuteczny. W pewnym momencie trafiamy na ścianę i przeciwnicy lub bossowie zaczynają być wyraźnie trudniejsi dla konkretnego stylu gry. W efekcie gracz zamiast rozwijać postać według własnej wizji zaczyna dostosowywać się do wymagań konkretnych walk. Oprawa wizualna i świat gry Pod względem artystycznym gra prezentuje się znakomicie. Świat jest ogromny, różnorodny i pełen charakterystycznych lokacji, a każdy region ma swój klimat i wizualną tożsamość. Na uwagę zasługuje również historia świata współtworzona przez George R. R. Martin. Lore jest ciekawy i intrygujący, choć duża część fabuły pozostaje ukryta w opisach przedmiotów i fragmentach dialogów. Dla jednych jest to element budujący tajemnicę świata, dla innych bariera w odbiorze historii. Problemy z kamerą Największą wadą gry jest kamera. To właśnie tutaj pojawia się najwięcej sytuacji prowadzących do frustracji. Podczas walki z przeciwnikiem można zablokować kamerę na celu. W teorii ma to pomagać w śledzeniu przeciwnika, ale w praktyce często prowadzi do chaosu. Kamera potrafi się gubić, nagle zmieniać pozycję albo ustawiać pod dziwnym kątem. W efekcie gracz nie widzi ani ataków przeciwnika, ani czasami nawet własnej postaci. Problem szczególnie nasila się przy dużych przeciwnikach. Kamera potrafi wtedy ustawić się tak blisko modelu bossa, że trudno ocenić sytuację na ekranie. Próba grania bez blokady celu również nie rozwiązuje problemu, ponieważ kamera nadal potrafi poruszać się samoczynnie i nie zawsze pozostaje tam, gdzie gracz chciałby ją ustawić. W praktyce oznacza to, że część zgonów nie wynika z błędu gracza ani z poziomu trudności walki, lecz z problemów technicznych i projektowych. Powtarzalność przeciwników i bossów Kolejną wadą jest design przeciwników oraz powtarzalność wielu walk. W wielu miejscach widać wyraźne użycie metody kopiuj i wklej. Boss, z którym wcześniej stoczyliśmy efektowną walkę, później pojawia się jako zwykły przeciwnik w innej lokacji. Osłabia to poczucie wyjątkowości starć i sprawia, że niektóre momenty przestają być tak znaczące, jak powinny. Walki bywają widowiskowe, ale to nie zawsze oznacza, że są dobrze zaprojektowane. Niektóre starcia sprawiają wrażenie mocno oskryptowanych. Czasami wygląda to tak, jakby można je było przejść sensownie tylko jednym konkretnym stylem gry, ponieważ inne podejścia są znacznie trudniejsze. Podejście do nowych graczy Gra nie szanuje również graczy, którzy wcześniej nie mieli styczności z tytułami typu Souls. W wielu momentach zakłada się, że gracz już zna mechaniki charakterystyczne dla tego gatunku. Systemy gry są słabo tłumaczone i wiele rzeczy trzeba odkrywać metodą prób i błędów. Popularność marki w dużej mierze opiera się na opinii o jej wyjątkowej trudności. W praktyce jednak spora część tej trudności wynika z problemów projektowych. Nieczytelność walki, problemy z kamerą czy niespójne decyzje designerskie sprawiają, że gra bywa wymagająca nie dlatego, że przeciwnicy są świetnie zaprojektowani, ale dlatego, że niektóre elementy gry utrudniają komfortowe granie. System punktów odrodzenia Dobrym przykładem niespójnego designu jest system punktów odrodzenia. Czasami ognisko znajduje się dosłownie przed areną bossa, a dodatkowo mamy jeszcze statuę, która pozwala odrodzić się jeszcze bliżej. W innych sytuacjach po każdej śmierci trzeba pokonywać długą drogę z ogniska do bramy bossa. Przy trudniejszych przeciwnikach, takich jak Malenia, Blade of Miquella, oznacza to, że spora część czasu nie jest poświęcona samej walce. Zamiast tego gracz biegnie z powrotem do areny i ponownie nakłada buffy przed starciem. W efekcie nawet jedna czwarta czasu spędzonego przy bossie może polegać po prostu na powtarzaniu tej samej drogi. Podsumowanie Elden Ring jest produkcją pełną kontrastów. Z jednej strony oferuje piękny świat, ciekawy lore i ogromne możliwości budowania postaci. Z drugiej strony cierpi na wyraźne problemy projektowe, takie jak praca kamery, powtarzalność przeciwników czy niespójne rozwiązania w designie walk. Nie jest to zła gra, ale zdecydowanie nie jest też tak bezbłędna, jak sugerują niektóre opinie. Część graczy wynosi ją na piedestał głównie ze względu na renomę studia FromSoftware, a niekoniecznie przez faktyczną jakość wszystkich elementów gry. To tytuł, który potrafi zachwycić wizją świata, ale jednocześnie momentami potrafi też bardzo frustrować.

I have played this game a lot, both with and without mods. I'll be blunt: it's a good game overall, but it has a lot of things dragging it down. Some say it's a 10/10 game, but I disagree. First of all, the biggest issue with this game, is input reading. Enemies and bosses don't react to what you do, they react the moment you press a button, before your action has even started. The enemy in Fort Gael is a good example: I try to shoot it with a crossbow, but it evade the moment I press the button, wether I'm aiming at it or not. This is dumb. -1 point. Next is wind-up attacks and tracking: a lot of bosses and enemies have ridiculous wind-ups that mess up dodge timing and ruins the rythm of the fight. And if you try to reposition to avoid it completely, they will simply turn around 180 degrees and hit you with that attack anyway. This is cheap, not difficoult. -1 point. Then there is the game balance: it feels like they spent less than 10 minuttes to balance this game. In a lot of late game areas, enemies are just basic scrubs that do nothing, while a mid game area might have enemies that will utterly destroy you regardless of stats and defence. Bosses also do WAYYYY too much damage in proportion to how often they attack and how long their combos are. They get to kill me in 2-3 hits while being able to chain 3-7 attacks in a row, while I'm lucky to land 1 single hit before they jump away from me and just stare at me from the other side of the area. This is utterly stupid. -2 points. Next is the ability to respec, upgrade weapons, and change builds: this is hopeless.... the game is incredibly stingy with upgrade materials, and even if you obtain the bellbearings, the mats get increasingly expensive. You need a total of 12 of each basic smithingstone to max a weapon, from lvl 1 stones to lvl 9 stones. And lvl 8 stones cost 30 000 runes a piece, just to give an example. This discourages experimentation in a game with over 100 weapons. Respecing is also limited, as there is a fixed amount of larval tears you can obtain in a single playthrough. This can hardlock you to stick with the same build through the whole game. -2 points. Now we are down to 4/10. Now lets add the good things: The world is big, with lots of things to discover around every corner. Everything from weapons, mats and spells, to catacombs, castles and dungeons. Exploration is very rewarding. +2 points. Buildvariaty: if we look away from the horrible upgrade system, there is a lot of different ways to build your character. You can go pure meele, or pure spell/incantation builds, or heavily focus on status buildup, or make a combination of either of them, and much more. +1 point. Encounters: there are many npcs to stumble upon in this game, most of wich leads to new side quests or detours, or even new areas. Some are missable, wich can lead to missing out on certain questlines or items, but this isn't really a problem. The npcs of this game are fairly interesting, and some will even fight alongside you at certain bosses if you summon them. +1 point. Now we are at 8/10. There is a lot more that drag this game both up and down, but these are my takes. Personally I give the game a 7/10. It's an overall good game, especially with certain mods, but it can be really frustrating at times, and I can't really think of anyone I would ever recommend this game to. I had my fun, along with much frustration. Edit: Steam doesn't ask if the game is good, Steam ask if I would recommend it. I would not, unless it is with mods.

Ludonarrative dissonance is a term used to describe the conflict between a game's story and its mechanics/gameplay. In the case of Stardew Valley, I have nothing but praise for the gameplay loops and design, blending almost every single possible element of classic games like Harvest Moon and Rune Factory into deep and fairly beginner-friendly farming experience with only a few minor exceptions. However, of all of Stardew Valley's flaws, I believe the greatest to be the aforementioned ludonarrative dissonance. Community building, anti-corporate sentiment, appreciation for a small-town lifestyle, and a return to simple living are prominently featured themes of the game, but basically every player ends up turning their own slice of small town heaven into an automated money printer that's filled to the brim with ways to get richer and richer. The game tells you to live a simple life, but so much of what you do in game is designed to increase the efficiency and output of your farm. That isn't to say that I believe the game is designed poorly, since I don't believe that at all. Rather, this is just a commentary on how people play games and constantly push the boundaries towards their logical extremes. After all, it's nice to have a farm with 80 green bean plants that you have to water every day by hand, but why settle for that when you can just do a little mining and have those 80 plants automatically watered by sprinklers? And once you have those sprinklers, why not make a few more? And so on, until you're planting 1678 Ancient Fruit on your farm to harvest a total of 15k fruit by the end of Fall and cycling through dehydrators, kegs, and casks to earn a roundabout figure of 22,665,000 for that calendar year. Fantastic game. Highly recommend.

This was my first ever FromSoftware game, and it was a great introduction to the souls games. Saying that this game is a 10/10 is an understatement. The open world is truly magical, straight out of a fantasy book (thanks George R. R. Martin). I can't go 10 steps on Torrent without finding a dungeon, beating the boss, and get either a mushroom, or a god-slaying weapon as a reward. The combat is stellar, and I could tell that the variety of builds is huge with the range of armaments, arts of war, talismans, and spells. Since this was my first souls game, the bosses were an extremely difficult, and the moment I tried to recuperate during combat, the bosses did not hold back to attack. Every boss and enemy spiked my focus, learning and avoiding their moves/abilities. All these factors would be for naught without the incredible music. Some of my favorite music comes from bosses such as Mohg or Godfrey, and the ambient music from Leyndell was not only soothing, but told a story of a great city in ruins after a war. There were many times of frustration, but the game improved my perseverance and patience. Before fighting Malenia, I thought I would beat her within 10 tries. 10 tries turned to 20 tries, and 20 tries turned to 2 weeks. Even after many defeats, I stilled fought, and through patience I eventually gained Malenia's Great Rune. To sum it up, it's a pretty fun game. 10/10

Overview: Cyberpunk 2077 is an ambitious open-world RPG set in a futuristic city (Night City). It delivers an incredibly immersive experience with strong storytelling and visuals—but it has also been criticized for technical issues and some underdeveloped gameplay systems. Pros 1. Immersive Open World Night City is widely praised as one of the most detailed and atmospheric game worlds ever created. Dense environments, strong world-building, and tons of side activities make it feel alive. 2. Stunning Graphics Incredible visuals, especially on high-end PCs with ray tracing. Lighting, reflections, and character detail are top-tier. 3. Strong Story & Characters Excellent writing and memorable characters enhance the narrative. Side quests are often as engaging as the main story. 4. Flexible Gameplay & Builds Multiple playstyles (stealth, hacking, combat) give players freedom. Deep RPG systems allow for character customization. 5. Voice Acting & Presentation High-quality voice acting and cinematic storytelling elevate immersion. Cons 1. Bugs & Technical Issues (especially at launch) Frequent glitches, crashes, and performance problems were heavily criticized. While many fixes have been released, reputation damage still lingers. 2. Some Gameplay Systems Feel Incomplete Melee combat and certain mechanics feel underdeveloped or “half-baked.” Balancing issues between different playstyles. 3. Main Story Length The main campaign is shorter than expected for an RPG of this scale. 4. Limited Impact of Choices Dialogue and choices don’t always significantly affect the world or story outcomes. 5. NPC & World Interaction Limitations Some players feel NPCs lack depth or realism compared to the environment. Final Verdict Rating: 9/10 If you want a deep, story-driven RPG with amazing visuals, this is a great pick. If you care most about polished gameplay systems and perfect performance, it may still feel inconsistent in places. Bottom line: Cyberpunk 2077 is a flawed but highly enjoyable game—one that delivers unforgettable moments, even if it doesn’t fully live up to its original hype. Highly replayable.

I wish I could like this game more, God knows I tried. It is very reminiscent of the way Morrowind made me feel many moons ago. It doesn't hold your hard, it encourages exploration, it encourages experimentation, the open world and world building are absolutely incredible, and it is overall extremely interesting. That said, just about everything else is insanely underwhelming. Obviously the game is insanely unfair towards the player. It isn't a hard game, it is an unfair game. Some people really like the feeling of accomplishment from beating their head against the wall for hours until it finally breaks, and I'm definitely not against a challenge, but what doesn't feel rewarding is defeating a boss because you got lucky. And sure, some things are worth suffering through for the reward, except there really isn't any reward other than saying you did it. There is clearly lore and some semblance of a story here, but there is absolutely no coherent storyline or characters for me to feel invested in whatsoever, which makes the idea of working through yet another insanely cheap and unfair boss encounter all the more uninteresting. I've played for over 65 hours this point and couldn't tell you why I'm doing anything in the game other than I guess because it's my destiny to do so or something? The insane thing is I'm actually the kind of player to go and explore and try to read and interact with everything I can. I will interact with every NPC and exhaust every dialogue trying to learn more about worlds like this that are very interesting, but there quite literally isn't a narrative at all. The combat feels pretty generic and uninteresting, like a more hardcore version of Skyrim. What is disappointing is I felt this way around 5 hours into the game but decided I would give it the good ole college try, but here I am at 65+ hours feeling the exact same. If you like the genre, you'll probably enjoy this. If you're okay with an insanely unfair challenge, give it a go. If you're looking for a truly wonderful open world experience with interesting boss fights, you'll easily get dozens of hours out of this game. If you're looking for a game with depth to really draw you into its world and immerse you, then this isn't it. It was fun working through some castles while watching videos on my second monitor. Definitely feels insanely overhyped. I'd probably give it a 6.5/10. If you like open worlds, RPG games, and aren't averse to challenge, maybe give it a try especially if its on sale. The real crime is if you don't play the game, you really aren't missing out on anything. No one is ever going to say "Whaaat, you didn't play Elden Ring!?"

While a few small details are perhaps missing, cyberpunk fans will love this game. - THERE IS SO MUCH DETAIL. Everytime you play this game again you find something new, and it really shows just how much work the devs put in when building the world. - You never run out of stuff to do. Even when you complete all the side quests and side content for this game, you can still find things tucked away in the nooks and crannies for you to explore. 3. The Combat - THRE IS INFINITE BUILD POTENTIAL IN THIS GAME. Whether you min max. or play a generalist, pretty much any build you can think of will be viable, and it always makes me want to go back and start over completely to try something new. You wanna play a tank that absorbs bullets and smashes gonks? You can do that. You wanna play a stealthy hacker that kills majority of enemies before combat even starts? You can do that. You want to be a total badass with a pistol and crazy movement? You can do that. You want to be a tank, hacker, and total badass? You. Can. Do. That. - The actual combat and gunplay in this game is soooooo unique. There's so many differentt ways to play. You can utilize cover and hit and run tactics with a stealthy build. You can bring a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ SWORD to a gunfight and utilzie crazy movement mechanics and hack away at gonks. You can do none of that, stare at people, and fry their brains before they can even unholster their weapon. Wanna be a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ cyber ninja with swords, throwing knives, and flys from enemy to enemy? DO IT. You wanna casually walk down enemies with a shotgun and (litterally) rip and tear through enemies like ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ doom guy?? DO IT. - All in all, never a dull moment in this game when it comes to shooting people, or cutting them open... 4. The Progression System - As stated before, this game has INFINTE BUILD POTENTIAL, and my favorite progression system of all time. Leveling up in this game feels sooooooooo goooood. A single perk can change the entire way you play, and once you start getting a lot of perks, you can start killing a lot of gonks, with the master level perks turning you into a total cyberpunk. - The attribute system is perfect. Opening certain areas or doing certian things in dialogue sometimes requires a certain amount of attribute points, litterally affecting your personality in game, which is CRAZY. 5. The Side Content - All of the gigs are unique and are well put together. All of them have some story element that is interesting and sometimes funny, and a lot of times ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up, which is the cyberpunk way. I never feel bored when doing the side quests, ESPECIALLY in the Phantom Liberty Expansion, where everything is turned up to the max. This game had a terrible launch, and it's a realy shame, because this game could've had the potential to surpass super big games like GTA. This game has improved so, so so much. I would reccomend the game to everyone, worth every single dollar 10 times over.

Forza Horizon 5 is a refreshing change of pace for gamers who are used to playing a lot of first- and third-person games (Halo, Assassin's Creed, God of War, etc.). There's no strategy, puzzles, or shooting involved, just an open road and world for you to drive around with, and without, friends. That doesn't mean that FH5 isn't challenging and adrenaline-inducing, because it is. Depending on how well you perform in your "career" and races (off-road, street, etc.) as you work toward the Hall of Fame, the game will shift you up difficulty levels, making races (which can be against AI's, I'll add) a bit harder. So, as you level up, so do those you race against. All that said, if you're looking for a "set" storyline with character development, awesome character cutscenes, and the whole story package, this game may not be it. FH5 is definitely a racing game with beautiful graphics and awesome cars, and I had a lot of fun in my '15 WRX STI, but there are times when you have many different storylines at once, which can get confusing and repetitive.

A Love Letter to the Lands Between If you are a fan of SoulsBorne games and you’re wondering if this is worth it—stop wondering. Get this game. It is an absolutely beautiful, massive masterpiece. To me, it feels like the ultimate "Greatest Hits" collection of FromSoftware; a perfect blend of the Dark Souls trilogy’s depth, the haunting atmosphere of Bloodborne, and the sharp DNA of Sekiro. What makes it special: True Freedom: The game gives you a little nudge at the start, but then the leash is off. You are free to roam a breathtaking open world filled with more items, gear, spells, and secrets than you’ll know what to do with. The Challenge: The bosses and enemies are legendary. Every corner of the map offers a new challenge that feels rewarding to overcome. A Quick Note for the Co-Op Travelers: If you want to experience this journey with friends without the constant threat of invasions, do yourself a favor: search for the "Seamless Co-op" mod and play your way: It deactivates the standard Easy Anti-Cheat (which, let’s be honest, you don't really want on your system anyway) and puts you on a private "server." You can set a password for your group and toggle invasions on (1) or off (0) as you see fit. Ignore the Gatekeepers: You aren't harming the official servers or bothering anyone else’s experience. If anyone tries to tell you off for choosing not to be invaded, let them cry. Those aren't "real" Souls players. Real players want you to enjoy the game. Bottom line: This is an incredible journey. Play it how you want, enjoy the world, and be happy. See you in the Lands Between!

Elden Ring completely pulled me in from the moment I first stepped into Limgrave. Seeing that massive world open up for the first time was honestly overwhelming in the best possible way. I remember just standing there, trying to decide where to go first, immediately making the questionable decision to wander off and explore [spoiler] before arriving at the first church [/spoiler]. That feeling of freedom is what makes this game so special. Every road, ruin, cave, or suspicious corner felt worth checking out because the game constantly rewarded curiosity. Even after hundreds of hours, I still kept finding hidden items, new paths, or entire areas I somehow missed before. The bosses and world design were easily my favorite parts. Getting destroyed by the Tree Sentinel early on was humiliating but hilarious, and it perfectly taught me what kind of game I was facing. Finally defeating Malenia after all the frustration, scarlet rot, and repeated failures felt incredibly satisfying. The game feels difficult, but fair, and every victory actually feels earned. I also loved diving into the lore, (even if most of it came from outside sources rather than the game directly - which is a personal choice in the end) Compared to Dark Souls III, this game takes everything I loved and pushes it much further. The open world, the freedom to explore, and even small quality-of-life improvements like traveling freely between Sites of Grace made the experience feel bigger and smoother without losing the soul of a FromSoftware game. Elden Ring may not be the hardest or fastest Soulslike ever, but it absolutely feels like one of the most memorable. It is one of those rare games where getting lost is not frustrating because it is the entire point. 10/10, currently replaying it too.

[h1]Hades[/h1] [h3]Overwhelmingly Repetitive and Overpraised Roguelite[/h3] [h3]Not worth trying[/h3] Hades is one of the worst slow-paced roguelites in the genre, it requires a lot of grinding to progress through a story that honestly doesn’t feel worth watching, since it’s a very average coming-of-age escape narrative set in a Greek mythology world from a fairly superficial perspective, taking a lot of awkward artistic and historical liberties. Personally, I think this title has been praised for the same wrong reasons. In reality It has a terrible progression system that feels monotonous and slow, colorful but incredibly flat visuals that affect gameplay readability, and an uninteresting story filled with too many side characters and subplots, making the story endlessly boring. [h3]Gameplay[/h3] As I mentioned before, the game is pretty repetitive and demands far too much time just to make a little progress. From the very beginning, it’s hard to reach the next area due to the poor starting equipment of our character, with limited abilities, terrible damage output and a mediocre health pool that barely gives any room to make mistakes and learn enemy attack patterns. It’s a very tedious game to learn, and the early difficulty walls feel unfair because you basically won’t have any truly useful upgrades to help you out unless you keep grinding resources, loss after loss. The game only becomes genuinely fun once you have enough upgrades to at least get through each area and actually experiment with different gods’ boons and synergies without constantly having to restart a run. Combat feels good overall, it’s fast and smooth with melee weapons. However, other options like the bow or the gunrail feel clunky and frustratingly slow, especially for a game with such fast enemies and close environments. On the other hand, the relationship system is slow and inconsistent, since it requires a lot of interactions just to complete a single storyline with a side character whose presence is, in some cases, low and often feels insignificant. [h3]Art and World Design[/h3] The game has a very vibrant visual style for its assets, characters and enemies. However, this artistic decision often gets in the way during combat. This title has a serious visual hierarchy problem. Most of its elements within the same scene share the exact same line quality and very similar color values, combined with an exaggerated lighting system that makes shadows and depth harder to read. As a result, many environmental obstacles feel flat and oversimplified, and it’s common to bump into them because of how poorly they blend into the environment. And then there’s the character design. Honestly, I think it was handled in a very poor artistic way, trying to justify their depiction under the excuse of a “reinterpretation” of Greek mythology by one of the developers, based on the idea that the Greek gods are not necessarily ethnically Greek. This is blatantly wrong and dishonest. It's pretty obvious that Greek gods are portrayed according to the ancient Greek canon standards, not foreign ones that have nothing to do with the culture they are trying to portray. [h3]Music and Sound effects[/h3] The soundtrack is energetic and playful, it’s genuinely enjoyable, and it’s easily one of the game’s strongest aspects. It’s the only aspect that actually integrates Greek culture well into the game using its typical instruments and melodies along with more modern arrangements.
